# The Failure of the 2030 Agenda

## Annual Congress of Xoán de Lugo, 2022. 5th Austrian-Galician Gatherings. Mondoñedo, Lugo, November 2022. {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}
{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YnJU9JOAi0c >}}
:::

Thank you very much, everyone. Welcome; it is an honor to be here with you. Since this is the opening lecture, it might not turn out perfectly, as I only had a month to prepare it, so let's see how it goes!

My talk today deals primarily with the energy transition. I am not going to question whether it is necessary or not. For the sake of argument, I will fully accept the official postulates regarding the necessity of an energy transition, the challenges of climate change, and so on. I will not dispute those premises, fundamentally because I lack the specialized knowledge to discern whether one stance or its opposite is correct. There are people here who know far more about the climate science than I do and can comment later, but I do not want to enter that debate. I take it as given: fine, suppose an energy transition must be carried out. What I intend to examine is whether the method chosen—namely, state central planning—is the appropriate vehicle to achieve that goal. I am not questioning the end itself; we can debate the end later. I am not qualified to say whether temperatures will rise by two, six, or eight degrees, or whether the planet will cool, because I simply do not know. I am not utterly ignorant of the matter, and I enjoy reading about it, but I observe highly qualified scientists on both sides of the issue. Therefore, I will align myself with the official narrative. I accept the UN, IPCC, and 2030 Agenda framework entirely. What I do understand, however, is central planning, incentive structures, public policy, and Austrian economics.

Before beginning, I would like to offer several caveats regarding how these issues are discussed. I have always been irritated by the careless importation of natural science concepts into social science. It invariably breeds confusion: concepts such as "friction," "equilibrium," or "evolution," when applied to human action, often obscure more than they illuminate. Cultural and institutional evolution operate on entirely different principles than biological evolution.

Similarly, I dislike when political concepts are grafted onto scientific discourse. Take "consensus": consensus is a political concept. Genuine consensus means unanimous agreement—every single person agrees. As the Poles knew well in their seventeenth-century Sejm with the *liberum veto*, consensus meant any individual deputy could veto legislation; a single dissent broke the consensus. When ministers today declare that "99% of scientists agree," that is not consensus—it is a supermajority, but not consensus.

Second, science is not democratic. We have grown accustomed to truth being decided by majority vote: a parliamentary committee votes by majority that a certain minister is culpable or that a disaster had a specific cause. Democracy may have its place in politics, but it has no jurisdiction over truth and falsehood. In science, the superior argument wins. That 99% say one thing and 1% disagree is an interesting indicator, but it is not proof of truth. History is replete with solitary dissenters who challenged unanimous scientific consensus and were ultimately vindicated after enduring fierce ostracism. Truth does not depend on headcounts; it depends on evidence and theoretical coherence. Even if 100% of scientists agreed at a given moment, that would not guarantee ultimate truth—any novel empirical discovery can dismantle a longstanding paradigm.

Furthermore, people tend to hypostatize abstract concepts. The other day I read about a scientist who felt offended because a politician questioned a climate prediction, claiming that the statement "offended Science." Come now: it may have offended you as a scientist, or offended your colleagues, but it did not offend "Science," an abstraction whom no one has had the pleasure of meeting! Just as when politicians claim a policy "offends the Spanish Nation"—it may offend individual Spaniards, but not the nation as a hypostatized entity.

Consider also the invocation of "the experts." People say: "We must listen to the climate experts." But "expert" is an ambiguous term. Expert in what? In climate debates, which expertise is paramount? The climatologist? The ecologist assessing biodiversity? The environmental economist like [Nicholas Stern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Stern%2C_Baron_Stern_of_Brentford)^[British economist, academic, and author of the Stern Review.] analyzing economic impacts? Political scientists like [Michael Klare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Klare)^[Professor emeritus of peace and world security studies.] studying resource conflicts? Or entomologists studying insect vectors? Which expert takes precedence, and how are their diverse assessments weighted when formulating policy? During the recent pandemic, governments routinely claimed to be "following the experts," yet upon inspection, those advisory committees were stacked with experts politically aligned with the governing party. When the IPCC or national bodies assemble expert panels, who selects them, and by what political criteria are they chosen?

Another fallacy is dismissing arguments based on funding: claiming that one scientist is bought by fossil fuel companies while another is pure. That is an *ad hominem* fallacy. If Shell finances a researcher's lecture, that fact alone does not invalidate the logical coherence of his arguments. A person acting out of financial interest may happen to state the truth, while someone with the purest moral intentions may be thoroughly mistaken. Arguments must be debated *ad rem*—on the merits of the proposition—not *ad personam*.

Having accepted the official premise that global temperatures must be regulated, the central question remains: how is this transition to be executed? Rulers have opted for a statist solution. If global consensus truly held that this was an existential catastrophe, one would expect voluntary behavioral adjustments. Citizens would freely curtail fossil fuel consumption, adopt frugal lifestyles, and purchase electric vehicles without coercion.

Philosophically, we could discuss whether property rights can exist in climate stability, as [Walter Block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Block)^[American Austrian School economist and anarcho-capitalist theorist.] has explored. Under private law, individuals could initiate tort litigation against specific polluting enterprises, demanding compensation for verifiable damages, much like class-action lawsuits against defective financial products. But that requires demonstrating tangible harm caused by a specific corporate actor.

People often object: "Citizens won't act voluntarily because they are myopic and selfish." But that reveals that people do not subjectively prioritize the climate threat as an urgent danger. If people genuinely believed coastal cities were imminent flood zones, beachfront real estate prices in places like Miami, Barcelona, or my native Galicia would already be collapsing! Real estate markets discount future risks: if buyers knew a property would be underwater in fifteen years, property values would plunge today. Yet beachfront property remains at record highs. Similarly, green investment funds that promised to decarbonize portfolios have largely underperformed, and investors have quietly retreated. As Nassim Taleb observes in *Skin in the Game* [@taleb2018skin], what counts in human action is not verbal professions, but where people actually allocate their capital.

Even governments demonstrate this revealed preference. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi declared that India would defer net-zero targets by twenty years. Xi Jinping noted, with typical Chinese pragmatism, that "one should not discard old shoes before acquiring new ones"—meaning China will not abandon coal until viable alternatives exist. And when tensions flared over Taiwan, Beijing promptly suspended bilateral climate talks with the United States. If climate catastrophe posed an imminent existential risk to monsoonal Asia, would national leaders play geopolitical poker with climate accords?

Since the public does not prioritize these mandates voluntarily, governments step in with central planning. We are told that supreme planning authorities will rationally engineer a decarbonized society. Here we confront the classic pitfalls of central planning. While not Soviet-style imperative planning, it resembles French indicative planning: a web of subsidies, tax penalties, quotas, and prohibitions. The British economist [Vera Lutz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vera_Lutz) demonstrated in her study of French planning [@lutz1965french] that indicative planning repeatedly failed to meet its targets due to fundamental knowledge and calculation problems.

First, central planners cannot control exogenous natural factors. Under Soviet [Gosplan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosplan)^[State Planning Committee of the Soviet Union.], five-year plans projected potato output and assigned trucks, fuel, and processing plants accordingly. If a single drought struck, the entire five-year plan collapsed: processing plants sat idle, trucks were stranded, and millions starved. Similarly, natural shocks like volcanic eruptions emit colossal quantities of greenhouse gases and ash, rendering bureaucratic carbon quotas instantly obsolete.

Second, state taxonomy of what constitutes "green" is arbitrary and politically volatile. Initially, only solar, wind, geothermal, and hydro were deemed acceptable. Suddenly, European regulators decreed that nuclear power was "green." Then, under diplomatic pressure, natural gas was labeled "green" so that green bonds could subsidize gas pipelines! When definitions shift overnight according to geopolitical expediency, market coordination breaks down.

Furthermore, environmental tax rates and carbon emission allowances are determined through bureaucratic bargaining rather than market pricing. The Russian economist [Boris Brutzkus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Brutzkus), whose *Economic Planning in Soviet Russia* [@brutzkus1982economic] independently identified the impossibility of socialist calculation alongside Mises, demonstrated that planning leads to systemic intertemporal discoordination. Capital goods require precise complementary inputs: Soviet factories produced tractors without batteries, or shoes without laces. Russian fishing trawlers sat in harbor fully manned because bureaucrats in Moscow forgot to requisition fishhooks!

A similar discoordination plagues current energy planning. Governments aggressively shuttered coal plants and nuclear stations before renewable capacity and transmission networks were mature. But solar and wind power are inherently intermittent: they depend on weather conditions beyond human control. When wind droughts and dry summers strike, output plummets. To maintain continuous grid stability, utilities must rely on dispatchable backup capacity—typically combined-cycle natural gas plants.

In European marginalist wholesale electricity markets, the price of the last megawatt-hour dispatched to meet demand sets the clearing price for all suppliers. While economically rational, this structure was intended to provide windfall revenues to amortize high-fixed-cost renewables. But when natural gas prices soared due to geopolitical conflicts and supply shocks, electricity prices skyrocketed across Europe. Terrified by voter backlash, governments executed a classic Austrian capital "reswitching"—reverting to primitive, dirty capital structures by reopening mothballed coal plants across Germany and Spain!

Notice the glaring intellectual contradiction: UN Secretary-General [António Guterres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Guterres) warned that humanity is "accelerating on a highway to climate hell." Yet the moment energy prices spike, European governments rush to burn coal, and when truck drivers threaten strikes, governments promptly subsidize diesel fuel by twenty cents per liter! If avoiding climate hell were truly the supreme civilizational emergency, wouldn't higher fossil fuel prices be welcomed as an effective market deterrent? By their actions, politicians reveal that winning the next election outweighs saving Gaia.

In *Fossil Capital* [@malm2016english], the eco-Marxist scholar [Andreas Malm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Malm) examines why British industry in the nineteenth century shifted from waterwheels to steam power. Water power was abundant and cheap, but intermittent and tied to specific river locations. Steam engines, though dirtier and reliant on expensive coal, offered modular, continuous power and could be erected near urban labor pools. Modern renewables suffer from the exact same spatial and intermittency constraints. While wind and solar are ingenious technological achievements, treating them as complete drop-in replacements for dispatchable baseload power ignores basic engineering realities.

As [Vaclav Smil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaclav_Smil) observes in *Energy Transitions* [@smil2016energy], modern fossil-fuel infrastructure—the global network of extraction fields, supertankers, pipelines, refineries, and grids—is the most colossal physical investment ever built by humanity. To suppose that this entire thermodynamic architecture can be dismantled and replaced by bureaucratic fiat within a few dozen years is pure techno-bureaucratic hubris.

Consider electric mobility. Degrowth theorists like [Antonio Turiel](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Turiel_Mart%C3%ADnez) in *Petrocalipsis* [@martinez2020petrocalipsis], [Alicia Valero](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alicia_Valero_Delgado) in *Thanatia* [@capilla2014thanatia], and [Carlos Taibo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Taibo) argue that a comprehensive global transition to electric vehicles is physically unfeasible due to mineral bottlenecks. Global reserves of lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper, and rare earths are insufficient to replace hundreds of millions of internal combustion vehicles, to say nothing of the colossal expansion required in electrical grid capacity.

Electric vehicles require an intricate, synchronized logistical ecosystem: widespread high-voltage charging networks, specialized repair workshops, battery recycling facilities, and spare parts pipelines. In addition, when only certain regions mandate electric cars while developing nations continue using combustion engines, manufacturers lose global economies of scale, keeping vehicle prices prohibitive for working-class families.

Most destructive of all is the disruption of the capital structure. As [Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_von_B%C3%B6hm-Bawerk) demonstrated, production processes are roundabout; capital structures extend across time. Arbitrary political deadlines—such as banning internal combustion sales by 2035—destroy capital value *today*, not a decade from now. What ambitious engineering graduate will dedicate twenty years to combustion thermodynamics when the field has been handed a death sentence? Universities shutter mechanical research programs, devaluing human capital.

Furthermore, these bans extinguish promising transitional technologies: synthetic e-fuels, [AdBlue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diesel_exhaust_fluid) emissions reduction systems, and hydrogen-diesel blends capable of retrofitting existing heavy engines. Refinery owners, told their operations must close by 2035, halt maintenance and capital investments immediately, triggering diesel supply crunches and refinery closures long before the deadline.

Moreover, if electricity is generated by burning coal or natural gas, an electric vehicle's lifecycle emissions can exceed those of a modern, highly efficient turbodiesel. Scrapping millions of roadworthy vehicles prematurely squanders the embedded energy and resources required to manufacture new cars, defeating the stated environmental objective.

Whenever consumer technologies genuinely improve human welfare—from smartphones to home computers—markets adopt them rapidly without subsidies, punitive mandates, or administrative decrees. If planners want electric mobility to succeed, they should encourage market innovation to produce an affordable, superior vehicle. Coercive central planning, rigid deadlines, and capital destruction will not prevent environmental degradation; they will merely guarantee economic impoverishment.
